'Diverging diamond' at I-89's Exit 16 will be open by end of the month
Poco in Burlington to Pause Dinner and Open for Lunch
Burlington police search for suspect in stabbing of a wheelchair user
Burlington Technical Center opens permanent home at new high school
stories.w: Six years after PCB concerns closed the old building, the Burlington Technical Center's five programs are finally back under one roof at the new Burlington High School, with additional offerings at the airport. Students walked into classrooms ranging from a criminal justice suite with an interrogation room to a health science academy built around a real-world hospital environment. Director Jason R

stories.t: Ribbon cutting celebrates completion of Burlington Wildways Trail
stories.w: Nearly ten years in the making, the ten mile Wildways Trail is officially complete, linking the Intervale, Ethan Allen Homestead, Ethan Allen Park and Rock Point in one continuous route from the Winooski River to Lake Champlain. Saturday's ribbon cutting at the Homestead ended the only way it should have, with a guided hike, and the full route is now open to everyone.

stories.t: Burlington mayor meets with businesses over downtown disorder
stories.w: A standing room only crowd packed City Hall on Friday as downtown businesses told Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak they are losing patience with open drug use, vagrancy and safety issues, with the Friendly Toast's manager describing a recent needle stick and Vermont Pub and Brewery reporting foot traffic down 20 percent from an already bad year. The mayor said she is not okay with the status quo and poi

stories.t: Why Vermont's housing shortage can't be explained by population size alone
stories.w: If the population is flat, why is it still so hard to find a place to live? This deep dive lands on household size, with 70 percent of Vermont households now just one or two people and the state average down to 2.2, one of the smallest in the country. The same number of people simply takes up more homes, and the Vermont Housing Finance Agency calculates the state needed nearly 22,000 additional ho

stories.t: Gov. Scott calls proposed 100-bed shelter in Chittenden County a bad idea
stories.w: The governor doubled down on his criticism of the City Council's 10-point homelessness resolution, saying he was surprised to see the 100-bed low barrier shelter on the list and that he would rather see smaller shelters spread across the county. He also suggested Vermonters elsewhere might be miffed at Burlington asking for extra resources when other regions face the same problems. Paired with Fri

stories.t: UVM president says school's budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment
stories.w: President Marlene Tromp used her first State of the University address to announce the projected $12 million deficit is fully closed, done through eliminating vacant positions and operational inefficiencies rather than layoffs. Enrollment is still the headwind, with about 2,600 first years against a usual target of 3,000 and roughly 10,800 students overall as the demographic cliff hits New England

stories.t: 49,000 Vermonters could lose Medicaid in the new year
stories.w: Federal Medicaid changes hit in waves, with several hundred immigrants losing eligibility October 1 and up to 49,000 Vermonters at risk on January 1 when new work requirements take effect, requiring at least $580 in monthly income or 80 hours of work, school, training or community service. Reviews also go to every six months starting in 2027. The state has launched StayCoveredVT.com so people can

stories.t: Abuse claimants fight Vermont Catholic Church plan to sell Rice Memorial High to supporters
stories.w: Lawyers for more than 100 clergy abuse claimants are challenging the diocese's plan to sell Rice Memorial High School to a supporter group for $4.3 million, just 14 percent of the $30.5 million value in the church's own appraisal, noting the property was never listed, brokered or opened to competing offers. The creditors want a public sale to raise more money for abuse settlements, while the dioce

stories.t: The Closures of Four Dairy Plants Lead to Worry in Vermont
stories.w: Four milk processing plants have closed or announced closures in a matter of months, in Barre, Georgia, Enosburg Falls and St. Albans, and the losses have farmers and state leaders worried about the $5.4 billion dairy sector's future. The St. Albans Creamery closure stings most, since the plant sold cream to Ben & Jerry's across town and its co-op owner had pledged $30 million in investment after

stories.t: 'I'll take money from anyone': Corporate cash fuels some Vermont political campaigns
stories.w: A Vermont Public analysis found Gov. Scott has taken $167,700 from corporations, businesses and corporate PACs over three cycles, 22.7 percent of his donations, while Attorney General Charity Clark has accepted $84,000, including checks from gambling companies and firms her office regulates or has sued. Both defend the practice, with Scott shrugging that there is no quid pro quo and Clark arguing

stories.t: Problem Properties: Burlington publishes list of noncompliant vacant buildings
stories.w: The city published a top ten list of noncompliant vacant buildings, naming properties like the old Bove's on Pearl Street, vacant since 2019 with violations that make it unsafe for emergency crews to enter, and a former gas station with no redevelopment plans. Owners on the list owe fees under the vacant building ordinance or have visible maintenance problems, and one landlord with two listed prop

stories.t: As Trump tries to curtail mail-in voting, Vermont officials clean up errors on state voter rolls
stories.w: The state removed just under 900 people from the voter rolls who were wrongly registered by DMV clerical errors going back 25 years, none of whom ever cast a ballot, all of whom had actively declined registration. Gov. Scott and Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas announced the cleanup themselves, framing it as getting the rolls airtight before general election ballots mail out next month, on

stories.t: New rules for Vermont vehicle inspections begin next month
stories.w: Starting September 1, your car can no longer fail inspection for rotor rust, tire cuts, windshield cracks or ABS and airbag warning lights, though mechanics can still recommend the fixes. If a station fails you solely for one of those, the DMV Highway Patrol says report it and they will investigate.

stories.t: Apps entice young Vermonters to join the 'birding boom'
stories.w: Free apps like Merlin Bird ID and eBird are pulling Gen Z into a hobby long associated with the 55 and up crowd, and the local numbers back it up, with UVM's ornithology class doubling to around 60 students a semester and campus Audubon chapters nationally growing from a dozen to over 92 since 2019. Young Burlington birders describe group chats that light up when a good bird shows at Colchester Po

stories.t: Smugglers' Notch installing 100 new snow guns for 70th season
UVM awarded $3.3 million to advance research on snow and outdoor economy
South Burlington pedestrian bridge site construction creates noise frustration
Snapping turtles to hatch soon at North Beach
Burlington Named the #3 Best US City to Work
stories.w: An Indeed study of metro areas over 200,000 ranked Burlington third in the country for work, behind only Boston and Washington DC and ahead of San Jose and San Francisco. The ranking weighed six pillars, from compensation to work-life balance, and our win came on job opportunity, where apparently Burlington posted the highest score in the nation. That’s an interesting one I didn’t expect, you agre

stories.t: ‘Watershed moment’: Vermont secures $92.7M and new restrictions for teens in Meta settlement
stories.w: Attorney General Charity Clark's 2023 lawsuit against Meta ended this week in the largest single-company settlement in state history, $92.7 million plus a decade of required protections for users under 18, including a nighttime block, a 2 hour daily limit, better age verification and a school mode that quiets notifications during the day. The deal was negotiated alongside 51 other states and terri

stories.t: Burlington Police arrest 11 people during month of drug operations in City Hall Park
stories.w: Burlington Police worked with the DEA and ATF on a multi-week covert operation in City Hall Park that produced 11 drug-related arrests between August 6 and 26, with plainclothes officers watching the park and its edges all month. Interim chief Shawn Burke wants to sustain the operations and tied that to the department's push for adequate staffing. The follow-through now shifts to the courts, prose

stories.t: Burlington Asks Again for State Help With Public Safety Problems
stories.w: In a rare moment of consensus, the City Council passed a unanimous resolution alongside Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak asking Gov. Phil Scott for immediate help on homelessness and public safety. The asks include support for a new 100-bed shelter in Chittenden County, faster access to the $83 million the Legislature set aside for emergency shelter overhaul, reversing the planned 70-day annual limit on

stories.t: Burlington artist dug Nap pleads not guilty in death of teen cyclist
stories.w: Douglas Knapp, 79, the folk artist known around town as dug Nap, pleaded not guilty Thursday to negligent operation with death resulting in the July crash that killed 16 year old Shiloh Skalka, a rising junior at Burlington High School riding her e-bike. The newly public affidavit says Skalka activated the flashing crosswalk signal at Pine and Locust, waited about 3 seconds, and was struck by Knap

stories.t: New students arrive at UVM as city, campus step up safety measures
stories.w: UVM move-in is underway, and both the university and the city are leaning into safety this year, with required safety modules before arrival, the CatSafe app connecting students to campus police or BPD around the clock, and a resource list from the mayor's office that includes a drug trafficking tipline. The first-years WCAX talked to said they feel safe on campus and plan to keep their heads up d

stories.t: Halfway through Vermont's first ever Navy Week
stories.w: Burlington Navy Week rolls on through Sunday, with ship demonstrations, live drills and daily Navy band music on the waterfront, plus a Navy presence at the fair starting today. Fewer than 100 active sailors call Vermont home, but the lake's naval history runs deep, and two vessels carry our city names, the fast-attack submarine USS Montpelier and the support ship USNS Burlington, currently deploy

stories.t: Rough pavement on I-89 caused by "raveling," VTrans says
stories.w: If you've felt your car wander in the right lane of I-89 between Montpelier and St. Albans, there's now a name for it. VTrans chief engineer Jeremy Reed says those grooves come from raveling rather than rutting, the top layer of pavement disintegrating so that in the worst spots you're driving on the layer underneath. The likely culprits are heavier traffic and a thin preservation treatment laid d

stories.t: 15 years after Irene, plucky business owners recall the monster storm and its aftermath
stories.w: Fifteen years ago today, Tropical Storm Irene sent rivers over their banks across Vermont, and this remembrance from Wilmington captures what that Sunday cost. Bartleby's Books took 3.5 feet of water and lost 85% of its inventory, roughly $400,000 in damage with less than half insured, and the flood line on Town Hall still sits a few inches above the 1938 record. stories.t: Vermont's bear population is booming. So is conflict with humans
stories.w: Vermont's game wardens have fielded roughly 1,800 bear calls so far this year, on pace for a record, and one bear in Jamaica ransacked a house and left the stove burner on. The population has more than tripled over 50 years to an estimated 7,500 to 8,900 animals, about double the state's target, so Fish and Wildlife wants to extend bear season into mid-December, allow two bears per hunter in parts

stories.t: Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown
stories.w: The 38 town listservs of the Upper Valley got a stay of execution. After Vital Communities announced it would stop supporting the two decade old email lists, community backlash bought a delay, and a group of residents and list managers is now forming a nonprofit called UV Lists to take them over this fall, with subscribers promised the same emails from a new domain for about $10,000 a year in tech

stories.t: Veterans Affairs to open clinic in South Burlington
stories.w: The VA signed a 20 year lease for a new outpatient clinic at Technology Park in South Burlington, expected to open by 2030 and replace the current Burlington clinic. The new spot puts roughly 7,900 veterans within an hour's drive, and the 24,000 square foot space adds mental health services plus physical and occupational therapy to the primary care, optometry and audiology already offered. Officia

Burlington prepares to host first-ever Navy Week
stories.w: Burlington Navy Week runs Monday through Sunday, the first Navy Week ever held in Vermont, and most of it is free and on the waterfront. A 34 foot Sea Ark harbor patrol boat does demonstrations off the Community Boathouse Monday and next Friday at 11:30, sailors from the namesake USS Montpelier and USNS Burlington are on display between ECHO and the Boathouse from noon to 5:30 Monday through Thurs

stories.t: Vermont's Miss Black USA reflects on historic win
stories.w: Harmony Edosomwan, who owns Harmony's Kitchen in Winooski and cooks traditional Black Southern food there, took home the national crown at this year's Miss Black USA pageant. Along with the title she won a full ride to law school, and she says she wants to use the platform to bring more attention to people of color living in Vermont.

stories.t: Vermont State Police patrols end in Burlington following violent weekend
stories.w: The state police pulled their extra downtown patrols Sunday after three weeks, an assignment Gov. Phil Scott ordered ahead of the New England governors and Eastern Canadian premiers conference. The weekend they left brought a stabbing near Bank and St. Paul, the fatal stabbing behind Courthouse Plaza, an exchange of gunfire on lower Church Street and a separate accidental discharge. Scott says the

stories.t: Suspect surrenders and faces second-degree murder charge in downtown Burlington stabbing
stories.w: Hassan O. Haji, 24, of Winooski, walked into Burlington police headquarters Tuesday morning and pleaded not guilty that afternoon to second degree murder in the Saturday stabbing behind the Main Street courthouse we noted Monday. Police allege that during a fight around 4 a.m. involving a third man, who has not been charged, Haji stabbed 24 year old Deng Dau once in the groin, and Dau died about a

stories.t: The Skinny Pancake Partners with Vermont Brewers in BTV and Quechee
stories.w: Starting today, the bar at the waterfront Skinny Pancake on Lake Street becomes a Lawson's Finest tap takeover that runs through foliage season, every tap pouring the Waitsfield brewery's beer, including the Sip line, with the new nonalcoholic Sip'N IPA in cans. The Quechee location has been running a Mount Holly Beer taproom since late June under the same idea. Both spots are posting suggested pa

Burlington High School opens new building in two weeks. Here's what's inside.
stories.w: Five years after PCBs pushed BHS students into the old downtown Macy's, the new building is ready, with a gym, an auditorium, soundproof music rooms, and an accessible balcony added from public feedback. It holds 1,100 students, comfortably ahead of the 960 currently enrolled across the high school and tech center. The ribbon-cutting is this Saturday, August 22, and the district is running free pu

stories.t: How Amanda Janoo, a progressive political outsider, won Vermont's Democratic primary for governor
stories.w: Janoo, an economist who had never run for office, took last week's primary 49.1 to 46.5 in unofficial results despite trailing Aly Richards in money and endorsements, and now faces Gov. Phil Scott in November. Analysts credit her plain talk on economic inequality and her read as the authentic change candidate, while a pro-Richards PAC's ad blitz, funded mostly from out of state, may have backfired

stories.t: Sneakers Bistro Goes Nighttime With Sneakeasy Cocktail Lounge
stories.w: Bar manager Yassen Zech and lead bartender Rachel Mutino designed the menu and the thrifted decor lounge together, with drinks like a clarified Bloody Mary martini and bar bites that nod to Belizean fry jacks. A series of soft openings leads up to the launch, and daytime service stays exactly as it was.

stories.t: Champlain Valley Fair comes to life with live artist demonstrations
stories.w: The fair's art exhibition (August 28 through September 6) is getting a gallery style refresh this year, with featured linocut printmaker Lauren McCabe and the Essex Art League carving and painting live for fairgoers. Around 500 public submissions get juried into categories that this year include Haunted and Just Desserts. If you want in, free online entry closes this Thursday, August 20, with drop

stories.t: Lake Champlain Chamber launches "Downtown Business Alliance"
stories.w: The Chamber's new advocacy division is meant to give downtown businesses a dedicated voice with city and state leaders as the core wrestles with public safety and economic uncertainty. It wants an advisory board seated by October 1 and is hiring a Downtown Advocacy Manager to track ordinances and represent businesses before the city council. Worth watching as budget season and the fall political c

stories.t: Three Teens Run the Show at Essex Junction's Black Ice Premium Ice Cream
stories.w: The scoop shop at 34 Park Street in Essex Junction is run by three brothers, 13-year-old twins Malachi and Messiah and 14-year-old Jaleel, who co-own it with their dad. They handle the scooping, the marketing, and the operations themselves, with ice cream from Woodstock's Mountain Creamery. Open daily 3 to 9 through October.

stories.t: South Burlington considers eminent domain for Long Property easement
stories.w: The city council is starting eminent domain proceedings for a road right-of-way on the 36-acre Long Property on Spear Street, where a 12-townhome Habitat for Humanity project is planned. The review board had to deny the application in July because the landowner would not include an easement for a future road the official city map requires, which started a 120-day clock for the city to act. City of

stories.t: Fluency gives infrastructure they need to trust AI
stories.w: The Burlington ad-tech company says its platform now drives $3 billion in annual ad spend across a quarter million monthly campaigns, with AI generating the creative while a deterministic layer keeps actual budgets inside advertiser guardrails. The company raised a $40 million Series A last year and just made the Inc. 5000 a fourth straight time. Granted, those are Fluency’s own numbers, but seein

stories.t: Montréal Critic Lesley Chesterman Shares Her Restaurant Intel
stories.w: Seven Days sat down with the Gazette's longtime restaurant critic, then built a 30-hour Montréal eating itinerary from her tips, from pastries at Rhubarbe to rotisserie chicken at La Lune to dinner at Le Violon. There is also a restaurant-history exhibit she helped instigate at the McCord Stewart Museum, running through October 18. If you have been meaning to make the drive north, this one doubles

stories.t: Plans to demolish old Bove's restaurant in Burlington put on hold
stories.w: The Bove family has pulled its permits to replace the old Pearl Street restaurant with a six-story, 25-unit housing building, citing interest rates, construction costs, and the wave of other housing projects underway in Chittenden County. The building has sat vacant since 2015 and ranks among the city's ten most non-compliant properties, but a city ordinance bars tearing down historic buildings wi

stories.t: A day in the life of a UVM Extension Master Gardener
stories.w: The Observer profiles Sue Stanne, a 23-year veteran of the program and one of 442 Master Gardener volunteers statewide, who spends Thursdays fielding plant mysteries on the Extension Helpline. Her projects run from the Vermont Respite House gardens to a donation plot at the Williston Community Garden to a new community gardening shed at The Farm at South Village. The helpline runs April through Oc

stories.t: 'Valley Transit' Films in the Upper Valley
stories.w: Believed to be the first feature film shot entirely in the Upper Valley, Valley Transit is filming with an all-local cast and crew as the centerpiece of a summer intensive that pairs students with professionals. The story follows a soon-to-be 80 man and a new high school grad who meet on a Valley Transit bus. Locals have lent homes and filled extra roles, and the project drew a grant from Vermont'

The results from Vermont's 2026 primary election
stories.w: Janoo, an economist who had never run for office, beat Aly Richards 49 percent to 46 percent as of 11 p.m. Tuesday. Molly Gray took the Democratic primary for lieutenant governor with 59 percent when the AP called it and will face incumbent John Rodgers in November. Gerald Malloy won the Republican U.S. House primary over Mark Coester and will challenge Rep. Becca Balint, who ran unopposed on the

stories.t: Chittenden County State's Attorney Sarah George prevails in hotly contested primary race
stories.w: George edged Bram Kranichfeld 15,931 votes to 14,923 after a campaign that pitted her progressive criminal justice record against his call for greater accountability in criminal cases. Down the ballot, Sheriff Dan Gamelin turned back challenger Kevin Bloom, 15,876 votes to 12,135. With nobody filed on the Republican or Progressive side in either race, Tuesday effectively decided both offices.

stories.t: After April fire, Williston ReStore set to reopen Aug. 15
stories.w: An April 23 fire closed Green Mountain Habitat for Humanity's Williston store for three months, and it reopens Saturday at 10 a.m. with a ribbon cutting and food, repaired, repainted and reorganized. ReStore revenue pays for Habitat's building work, including three homes going up right now at Harvest Crossing in Underhill, with 11 homes in the pipeline and a goal of up to 15 under construction by

stories.t: Vigil and Ride for Teen Cyclist Killed in Crash Draws Hundreds
stories.w: Some 500 cyclists rode a two mile circuit Wednesday evening from Pine and Locust streets, where a white ghost bike now marks the spot 16 year old Shiloh Skalka was struck on July 16. Driver Douglas Knapp, cited for negligent operation with death resulting, is due in court August 27, and speakers urged the community to attend the arraignment. A memorial fund set up by Skalka's family has topped $10

stories.t: Healthcare workers plan picketing outside UVM Medical Center
stories.w: AFT Vermont says the unions have been bargaining with the hospital since April for livable wages and improved staffing enforcement, and the expired contract means work stoppages and pickets are now legal. Look for the picket line at the main entrance today.

stories.t: Feds Sue Vermont for Giving Undocumented Residents the In-State Tuition Rate
stories.w: The federal lawsuit challenges Vermont's year old law giving undocumented residents in-state rates, a difference of about $17,000 versus nearly $47,000 a year at UVM. Vermont is now among 17 states the DOJ has sued over such laws, and the complaint claims, dubiously per Seven Days, that as many as 10,000 undocumented students attend Vermont colleges, which would be about one in four. Attorney Gene

stories.t: St. Michael's College accreditation at risk amid steep enrollment drop
stories.w: The New England Commission of Higher Education issued the Colchester college a formal notation this summer after full time undergraduate enrollment fell from 1,539 in fall 2019 to 1,021 in fall 2025. Commission president Lawrence Schall says the school still meets its standards and that losing accreditation would take many more steps. stories.t: Officer Who Called Border Patrol to Traffic Stop Was Working for the Feds at the Time
stories.w: The Chittenden County sheriff's sergeant who summoned Border Patrol during a July 19 traffic stop, leading to the deportation of a 22 year old dairy farmworker, was working a federally paid Operation Stonegarden overtime shift at the time. Records obtained by Seven Days show Vermont agencies received $760,000 through the border security grant program in fiscal 2024, with the Chittenden County Sher

stories.t: UVM Health faces massive losses despite major cost cuts
stories.w: The network told state regulators it expects to lose more than $14 million next fiscal year on roughly $3.16 billion in revenue, the first budget in recent memory submitted with a negative operating margin, and UVM Medical Center alone projects a $43 million loss. The plan already includes $140 million in expense cuts, fewer traveling nurses and a new 36 hour weekly minimum of patient facing time

stories.t: Burlington Free Press staff in union protest over 'snooping'
stories.w: A community contributed Patch post reports that the NewsGuild, which represents Burlington Free Press staffers, is protesting a new data partnership between parent company USA Today Co. and Palantir, announced on the company's second quarter earnings call as a way to collect and monetize audience data. The guild's objection, per the post, is that details of the partnership and protections for read

stories.t: 'Queen City Songs,' David Schein's Musical Tour of Burlington
stories.w: Burlington native David Schein, who turns 77 this month and once wrote and toured with Whoopi Goldberg, premiered his new performance piece Thursday at Off Center for the Dramatic Arts on North Avenue, with shows through Saturday and more August 20 through 22. The show blends original songs and unscripted stories into a musical walking tour of the city, from childhood haunts on North Prospect Stre

Data: Only 3% of Vermont registered voters have cast their ballots ahead of the primary election
stories.w: Tomorrow is primary day, and as of late last week only 3 percent of registered Vermont voters had returned a ballot. Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas is publishing early turnout numbers for the first time as a nudge, with Shelburne among the few towns beating the average. The practical part for Monday readers is that it is now too late to trust the mail, so hand your absentee ballot to you

stories.t: Mirabelles Bakery to Take Over Both Kitchen Table Locations
stories.w: Both Kitchen Table spots closed earlier this month, and Mirabelles is taking over the pair, the restaurant in Richmond and the market on Williston Road in South Burlington, with reopenings targeted by the end of September. The Richmond spot will likely become 'Belles on the River, serving casual dinners Wednesday through Sunday plus weekend brunch with the popovers along for the ride. One thing wo

stories.t: South End residents suggest ways to make biking safer, following teen death in e-bike crash
stories.w: Local Motion held its first walk-bike forum steps from the Pine Street memorial for 16 year old Shiloh Skalka, who died in July after being struck while riding her e-bike. Neighbors marked dangerous intersections on city maps and pitched fixes like new crosswalks, with Councilor Becca Brown McKnight calling the moment a wake-up call and saying the city is not doing enough. The driver has been cite

stories.t: Athletes at the Vermont Ninja Warrior Training Center Aim for the Big Time
stories.w: The Vermont Ninja Warrior Training Center moved into its own 7,200 square foot gym in Essex this spring, and three of its own are on the current season of American Ninja Warrior, including comanager Amir Malik of Essex Junction, who made the National Finals. About 300 students train there weekly, with kids starting as young as 4 and a 44 athlete competitive team that has traveled as far as Barbado

stories.t: Ray's Seafood Market and Restaurant closing after 74 years
stories.w: Ray's Seafood in Essex Junction announced this weekend it will close after 74 years, with the last day of service set for September 12. The family business started as a wholesale seafood provider 74 years ago and gave no reason for the decision. There is a month left to get a final basket of fried clams, and if you have a gift receipt the ask is to use it before the doors close.

stories.t: One month in, Champlain Parkway draws both praise and complaints
stories.w: Five weeks in, drivers love how fast the Parkway gets them to the highway, and Pine Street is paying for it with new backups. The top complaint is the missing left turn arrow where the project swapped four-way stops for signals at King and Maple, with waits of up to three light cycles at peak times. DPW is collecting signal data and owes the City Council findings and recommendations within six mon

stories.t: Chefs and servers on the Champlain Valley Dinner Train keep service on track
stories.w: Community News Service rode along in the kitchen car of the Champlain Valley Dinner Train, where four cooks plated nearly 170 three course dinners on a single evening run. The train now rolls all the way to Middlebury on a three hour round trip from Burlington, with Rutland's Southside Steakhouse catering as it has since 2018 and servers logging up to 25,000 steps a shift. The season runs through

stories.t: Queen City Public Safety Debate Shifts to Needle Exchanges
stories.w: The downtown safety fight has narrowed onto harm reduction, after the council's Burlington Forward resolution passed 7 to 5 with zoning language aimed at keeping syringe programs and the planned overdose prevention center out of downtown. The flashpoint is Vermont CARES' expanded Bank Street exchange, which opened July 1 with state backing after the Howard Center's Clarke Street program closed und

stories.t: A chastened UVM Health embarks on its first budget season after leadership reset
stories.w: UVM Health is back before the Green Mountain Care Board with a message of contrition, pointing to a new CEO, executive cuts, paused bonuses, a 12 percent price reduction in its BlueCross contract and dozens of layoffs. The system still projects a $14.7 million loss next year, with the Burlington flagship down $43 million, and its proposed expense growth remains more than triple what regulators sug

stories.t: Burlington mid-year housing market review
stories.w: The mid-year Redfin numbers show the Burlington market finally exhaling, with the median sale price down 4.2 percent from last year while the national figure rose. Active listings are up 19.4 percent, homes now sit a median 48 days before selling, and the share going above asking has slipped. Nobody would call $466,000 affordable, but after years of frenzy, more choices and longer decision windows

stories.t: Majestic Chef Micah Tavelli to Leave Burlington for a Big-City Gig
stories.w: Micah Tavelli, the James Beard semifinalist behind the stoves at Majestic in the South End, is leaving to run the kitchen at a Danny Meyer group restaurant opening in Boston's Seaport. His last day is this Saturday, so the week ahead is your window for one more Tavelli-era dinner. Dan Schloemer, his former sous chef, takes over with the menu expected to hold steady through the fall.

stories.t: Healthy Living appeals labor board decision upholding employee union
stories.w: Healthy Living has filed a roughly 700 page appeal asking the national labor board to throw out its workers' 105 to 69 April union vote, alleging a coordinated infiltration campaign by organizers. Two of the named baristas were fired the day before a union press conference, which the company attributes to guest complaints and the workers attribute to organizing. stories.t: Annual recovery summit aims to explain the unexplainable
stories.w: The fifth annual Coming Together, There is Hope summit drew an estimated 2,000 people to the Champlain Valley Expo at the end of July, including the lieutenant governor and a federal judge speaking on addiction in her courtroom. Vermont carries some of the highest substance use rates in the country, and about 70 percent of people incarcerated here receive medication assisted treatment. The message
